Abstract
This paper proposes the multiplier leadership optimization algorithm, which draws inspiration from multiplier leadership 
principles to search for and optimize solutions to complex problems effectively. Multiplier leaders possess the unique 
ability to amplify their teams’ collective intelligence and capabilities. They cultivate an environment of open discussion, 
creative thinking, accountability, and motivating team members to excel. The proposed algorithm is implemented in MAT-
LAB, and its performance is evaluated on the IEEE Congress on Evolutionary Computation 2021 test bench suite, which 
consists of 80 benchmark functions. The performance of the proposed approach is compared with those of the other 
9 other state-of-the-art optimization algorithms. The proposed algorithm successfully solved 47 out of 80 benchmark 
functions, demonstrating its superior performance. The computational complexity of proposed algorithm is O(M ∗N2) , 
making it efficient for large-scale problems. Furthermore, this paper proposes an MLOA-based approach to evolve the 
near-optimal architecture of convolution neural networks for Melanoma classification. The proposed approach is imple-
mented in Python and tested on the PH2 and ISIC2020 datasets. The PH2 dataset consists of 200 dermoscopic images, 
while the ISIC2020 dataset comprises 33,126 images. The proposed approach is compared with 12 other state-of-the-art 
methods and achieves high classification accuracies of 98.97% on the PH2 dataset and 99.47% on the ISIC2020 dataset. 
Additional performance metrics include precision of 98.72%, recall of 98.85%, and F1-score of 98.78% on the PH2 data-
set, while on the ISIC2020 dataset, it achieves precision of 99.32%, recall of 99.51%, and F1-score of 99.41%. The results 
indicate that MLOA-based CNN architecture outperforms all existing approaches for Melanoma classification, offering a 
promising solution for medical image analysis.

•	 Introduces MLOA, a novel optimization method inspired by multiplier leadership principles.
•	 MLOA outperforms 9 existing algorithms across benchmark functions.
•	 Achieves superior Melanoma classification accuracies up to 99.47% on diverse datasets.

1  Introduction
Leadership is a fundamental element of organizational success, is pivotal in shaping team dynamics and achieving 
optimal outcomes. It encompasses vision, communication, adaptability, and a deep understanding of team dynamics. 
Multiplier leadership is a transformative approach that has resulted in a remarkable 2X improvement in performance, 
nearly doubling the output compared to that of ordinary circumstances [1].
In leadership styles, a critical dichotomy emerges between two distinct approaches: Multiplier Leadership and Dimin-
isher Leadership. Multiplier leaders are known for extracting the best from their teams. They create an environment where 
individual strengths are magnified, fostering a culture of empowerment, continuous learning, and accountability. They 
leverage collective intelligence, encourage creative thinking, and promote trust and respect. In contrast, Diminisher 
leaders often act as sole contributors, monopolizing decision-making and undermining the capabilities of their team 
members. They may inadvertently create an environment marked by self-doubt and insecurity [1].
Multiplier leadership is a transformative approach to leadership that has gained recognition for its profound impact 
on team dynamics and performance. Unlike traditional leaders, multiplier leaders possess a unique set of attributes that 
enable them to amplify the capabilities of their teams. They are characterized by their keen ability to learn continuously, 
not only about themselves but also about their team members, the strengths and weaknesses of their competitors, and 
the ever-evolving landscape of markets and customers. This commitment to perpetual learning fosters an environment 
in which team members are motivated to enhance their skills and capabilities autonomously. Multiplier leaders excel 
in facilitating discussions before making decisions, encouraging analytical and creative thinking by posing challenging 
questions, and holding team members accountable for their actions. They instill a sense of intensity, invite full attention 
and effort, and inspire team members to take ownership of their work. Importantly, multiplier leaders are not perpetually 
upbeat or positive, as they understand that challenges and setbacks are part of growth [1]. This paper proposes a new 
algorithm, the multiplier leadership optimization algorithm (MLOA), which is inspired by the concept of the principles 
of multiplier leadership to search for and optimize solutions for complex problems. In this paper, we propose an MLOA-
based approach for melanoma detection and classification.
Traditional optimization techniques such as PSO, GA, GWO, and WOA have demonstrated significant efficiency in 
global optimization problems. However, these methods suffer from challenges like premature convergence, imbal-
anced exploration–exploitation mechanisms, and inefficient handling of complex multimodal landscapes. PSO and 
GWO often converge prematurely due to stagnation in local optima, whereas GA can be computationally expensive due 
to repeated crossover and mutation operations. WOA’s exploitation mechanism is highly dependent on its encircling 
strategy, which may lead to suboptimal solutions in high-dimensional spaces. In contrast, the Multiplier Leadership Opti-
mization Algorithm (MLOA) introduces a novel team-driven approach, leveraging leadership dynamics to guide solution 
search more effectively. By integrating collaborative decision-making, discussion-driven refinements, and leader–fol-
lower dynamics, MLOA achieves a superior balance between exploration and exploitation, leading to more robust and 
efficient optimization.
Melanoma is one of the most prevalent and fatal cancer types and has experienced a significant global surge. Failure 
to identify this mutation at an early stage elevates the risk of metastasis, contributing to elevated fatality rates. Early 
detection of this disease offers a potential cure for melanoma. Hence, a crucial focus of ongoing research involves the 
prompt and precise identification of these cancers. Various technologies within the realm of machine learning have found 
applications in facilitating intelligent melanoma detection. Machine learning makes the models and algorithms capable 
of learning from familiar data and making predictions based on unfamiliar data instances. In contrast, the conventional 
biopsy method employed for melanoma diagnosis is both laborious and costly.
Skin cancer arises due to the development of irregular cells, which are capable of infiltrating or propagating 
into different parts of the body. Skin is the organ most exposed to environmental pollutants making it susceptible

Metaheuristic optimization techniques have emerged as powerful tools for enhancing the performance and 
efficiency of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and other ML models. Unlike traditional optimization methods 
that may struggle with high-dimensional and nonlinear datasets, metaheuristics excel in handling such complexi-
ties by balancing exploration (searching widely across the solution space) and exploitation (exploiting promising 
solutions). For instance, GA mimics the process of natural selection to evolve candidate solutions over generations, 
while PSO simulates the behavior of bird flocks or swarms to iteratively refine solutions based on social interactions. 
These algorithms are particularly beneficial in fine-tuning hyperparameters, optimizing network architectures, and 
improving model generalization across diverse datasets. By integrating metaheuristic optimization into CNNs and 
ML models, researchers can achieve superior performance in tasks such as image classification, object detection, 
and medical diagnosis, thereby advancing the capabilities of AI-driven technologies in real-world applications.

models are adept at addressing intricate problems efficiently. Deep neural networks (DNNs), CNNs, long-term 
short-term memory (LSTM), and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are widely used deep learning approaches 
for melanoma detection [9]. In this paper, we developed the near-optimal architecture of a CNN using MLOA for 
melanoma detection.

2  Literature review
Machine learning model development represents a critical challenge in the field of artificial intelligence, with opti-
mization playing a pivotal role in achieving robust and efficient solutions. This literature review explores various 
optimization approaches and their applications in machine learning, with a focus on the emerging paradigm of 
the multiplier leadership-based unconstrained global optimization algorithm (MLOA). Optimization serves as the 
backbone of machine learning model development. The selection of model structures and parameters involves an 
intricate optimization problem aimed at minimizing the error between predicted and actual outputs [10]. As data 
complexity and nonlinearity increase, traditional optimization methods become inadequate, necessitating the adop-
tion of soft computing techniques [11].
The problem of developing a machine learning model consists of two steps: the first step involves identifying the 
“ n ” input “ m ” output model from the given training data, and the second step involves implementing the model. The 
first step can be considered an optimization issue in which the model structure and parameters are selected such 
that the error between the predicted output by the model and the desired target values specified in the training 
data is subject to a set of constraints [12]. Any of the minimization algorithms can be applied for the identification 
of such systems. However, for complex and nonlinear data, these problems turn out to be NP-hard problems, which 
necessitate the use of soft computing approaches to resolve the issue [13].
Soft computing encompasses a suite of methodologies tailored for approximate reasoning and ideally suited for 
tackling complex, nonlinear problems in machine learning [14]. These methods include fuzzy logic-based systems, 
artificial neural networks (ANNs), granular computing, rough sets, and an array of search and optimization algorithms 
[15]. Soft computing approaches are based upon approximate reasoning, in contrast to hard computing approaches, 
which are based upon exact reasoning [14]. Soft computing is an umbrella term consisting of methodologies and 
approaches such as fuzzy logic-based systems, ANNs, granular computing, rough sets-based computing, and the 
number of search and optimization algorithms.
Evolutionary computing, which encompasses genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization, and evolutionary 
strategies [16], stands out as a prominent category of optimization algorithms. These algorithms mimic the princi-
ples of biological evolution to search for optimal solutions, making them adaptable for diverse machine learning 
tasks [17]. The literature is rich in search and optimization algorithms that can be suitably adapted to identify an 
optimized model. The search and optimization algorithms can be broadly classified into 5 classes: evolutionary com-
puting, swarm intelligence (SI) approaches, bioinspired non-SI approaches, physics/chemistry-based approaches, 
and others [18]. In addition to SI, bioinspired optimization algorithms include simulated annealing, harmony search, 
and cuckoo search [19]. These methods draw inspiration from various biological and natural phenomena, providing 
versatile tools for machine learning model development [20]. Physics and chemistry-based optimization algorithms, 
such as the firefly algorithm and chemical reaction optimization, have demonstrated promise in addressing complex 
optimization problems [21].
The MLOA represents an innovative approach rooted in multiplier leadership principles. MLOA integrates the 
dynamics of leadership and team interactions to explore and exploit optimal solutions [1]. This approach leverages 
leader-team discussions, creative thinking, accountability, and the multiplication effect of leadership to generate 
improved candidate solutions iteratively. The application of MLOA in machine learning model development signi-
fies a novel avenue. By incorporating leadership dynamics and team learning into the optimization process, MLOA 
promises to enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of model identification and implementation.

box methods for feature extraction. Feature reduction was performed using LDA techniques, and among the four 
classifiers used, KNN demonstrated the highest precision (86%) and specificity (99.9%).
Vipin et al. developed a two-stage system focusing on segmentation and classification to diminish human involve-
ment in melanoma diagnosis, decreasing the degree of error and time [23]. Their approach involved utilizing an ISIC

3  Proposed multiplier leadership optimization algorithm (MLOA)
In algorithm development and optimization, effective leadership principles can provide invaluable guidance. Leadership 
extends beyond mere authority; it embodies the ability to inspire, guide, and empower individuals and teams to reach 
their full potential. This substantial enhancement is attributed to the unique attributes of Multiplier Leaders, which are 
encapsulated in a structured performance enhancement process:
1. Posing the Challenge: At the core of the Multiplier Leadership process lies the ability to pose a challenge effectively. 
The Multiplier Leader articulates and frames the team’s goals as challenges that demand innovative solutions. This 
initial step serves as a rallying point for the team, igniting their problem-solving spirit.
2. Discussion, Debate, and Formulation of Preliminary Plans: Building upon the challenge, the Multiplier Leader initiates 
a collaborative discussion within the team. Each team member is encouraged to contribute ideas and suggestions 
to fulfill the overarching goals. This phase marks the inception of a new project. The leader fosters an environment 
where ideas are freely shared, solutions are rigorously debated, and the team’s creative power is harnessed. Through 
this collective effort, a diverse array of candidate solutions emerges, embodying team members’ wisdom, experience, 
skills, and capabilities. This collection of ideas forms the P0 set, a pool of feasible candidate solutions to achieve the 
team’s objectives.
3. Selection and Refinement: With the wealth of ideas gathered in P0 , the Multiplier Leader, employing their judgment, 
identifies the most promising plan. This chosen plan serves as the foundation for further development. Here, the Mul-
tiplier Leader leads the team in the creation of P1 , a set of refined candidate solutions. The focus shifts to optimizing 
and enhancing the selected plan to align with the team’s goals.
4. Invoking Analytic and Creative Thinking: The Multiplier Leader invokes analytic and creative thinking to extract 
maximum value from every team member. Each team member is tasked with evaluating the plans within P0 . This 
evaluation process is designed to elicit the desired changes and optimizations for each plan in P0 . The result is a

3.2  Unique characteristics of MLOA compared to existing metaheuristics
The Multiplier Leadership Optimization Algorithm (MLOA) differs from other metaheuristics in both inspiration and 
execution strategy. Unlike conventional bio-inspired algorithms such as PSO, GA, WOA, or GWO, which simulate natural 
phenomena or animal behaviors, MLOA is inspired by human leadership dynamics. This provides several unique advan-
tages. While PSO mimics bird flocking and GA draws from genetic evolution, MLOA mimics how effective leaders guide 
teams, encouraging open discussion, critical thinking, and accountability—elements absent in traditional metaheuris-
tics. In MLOA, each candidate solution is treated as a “team plan.” These plans are refined collaboratively through team 
discussion and leader-member interactions, allowing for dynamic refinement of decision variables—contrasting with 
PSO’s fixed update rules or GA’s stochastic mutations.
MLOA introduces a novel operation where each plan is re-evaluated not just by perturbation or crossover but by 
creatively generating alternatives based on previous iterations, similar to how a team improves ideas over time. Many 
algorithms (e.g., PSO, GWO) tend to converge prematurely due to a rapid shift toward best solutions. MLOA maintains 
diversity by exploring alternative paths through creative team thinking and leader-based adjustments. MLOA follows a

4  Proposed MLOA‑based approach for melanoma classification
This section proposes the MLOA-based approach to evolve the near-optimal architecture of CNNs for melanoma clas-
sification. CNNs are essential for tasks such as image classification and object detection, but their performance heavily 
relies on the configuration of hyperparameters, such as learning rates, batch sizes, and network architectures. These 
hyperparameters are often challenging to fine-tune, given the intricate relationships between them and the high dimen-
sionality of the search space. MLOA draws inspiration from Multiplier Leadership, an influential leadership style known 
for maximizing team potential. The method approaches the optimization of hyperparameters as an analogous process 
to optimizing the capabilities of a team. Table 6 presents the upper and lower hyperparameter limits for evolving CNNs 
using the proposed bioinspired algorithm.
The algorithm starts with an initial set of hyperparameter configurations. The settings of each hyperparameter are 
mapped to a team plan, where each hyperparameter represents a decision variable. These plans are randomly generated 
to form the initial team proposals. A team leader is randomly chosen from the initial set of team plans. This leader serves 
as a reference point for the team’s evolution. The MLOA continuously explores new hyperparameter configurations by 
perturbing team plans’ decision variables (hyperparameters). The leader interacts with team members (hyperparameters) 
to selectively modify their decision variables based on a multiplier probability. This process encourages convergence 
toward optimal hyperparameters. An evaluation function is often based on CNN model performance; in our case, it is 
the model’s accuracy and assesses the fitness of each hyperparameter configuration. The algorithm selects the best-
performing hyperparameter configurations from the prospective set of team plans. A new team leader is chosen from 
this elite group. The global plan is updated with the decision variables of the new team leader, reflecting the evolving 
optimal hyperparameter settings. Steps are repeated iteratively until a termination criterion is met, such as a maximum 
number of iterations or a desired accuracy threshold is reached.

5  Algorithm steps
Step 1: Initialize Parameters: Create an initial set of hyperparameter configurations, H0 . Set the iteration counter, 
iter to 0.
Step 2: Generate Team Plans: Map each hyperparameter configuration in H0 to a team plan. Each hyperparameter 
corresponds to a decision variable in the team plan. Randomly generate a set of N team plans, forming the initial 
set of team proposals, P0.
Step 3: Team Leader Initialization: Randomly select one team plan as the team leader, TL . Initialize the global plan 
with the decision variables of the team leader, Global_Plan = TL.
Step 4: Iterative Optimization: While the termination criterion is not met (e.g., maximum iterations or desired 
accuracy is not achieved), the following steps are performed:
a. Team evolution
For each team plan P in P0 , create a set of new plans, P1 , by perturbing the decision variables (hyperparameters) 
of P . Team members (hyperparameters) use their creativity and information to update their decision variables, gen-
erating another set of plans P2.

b. Leader interaction
The team leader TL interacts with the team members (hyperparameters) and selectively modifies their decision variables 
based on the multiplier probability, Pm . For each decision variable, if the value of the team variable ( {Virtual_P2}_{i_j} ) 
differs from that of the global plan ( {Global_Plan}_j ), we determine whether to modify the decision variable based on 
Pm . If Pm is less than or equal to Member_Mult_prob , the team member’s decision variable is replaced with that of the 
team leader, encouraging convergence. A new set of virtual plans or proposals named {Virtual_P3}_{i_j} represents the 
multiplying effect of the leader on the team.
c. Combine proposals
The original set of proposals ( P0 ) is combined with all virtual teams ( virtual_P1 , virtual_P2 , virtual_P3 ) to create a 
prospective set of team plans.
d. Evaluate fitness
The fitness of each plan (hyperparameter configuration) in the prospective set was evaluated using an evaluation 
function (e.g., accuracy of CNN models).
e. Select new team plans
Select the N best plans (individuals) from the prospective set of team plans based on their fitness scores. Set Pnew as 
the new set of team plans.
f. Update global plan
Update the global plan ( Global_Plan ) with the decision variables of the new team leader ( TL ) selected from Pnew.
g. Iterate
The iteration counter ( iter ) is incremented by 1.
Step 5: Results and Termination: Display the optimized hyperparameter configuration H_opt corresponding to the 
decision variables of the final team leader. Terminate the algorithm.
By summing all the individual complexities, the overall algorithmic complexity of the MLOA is approximated as 
O(N ∗(M + log(N))) , where N is the number of initial configurations and M is the number of decision variables (hyper-
parameters) in each configuration.
5.1  Hyperparameter optimization strategy using MLOA
In the proposed framework, MLOA was employed to automatically optimize the hyperparameters of the CNN architecture 
used for melanoma classification. Key hyperparameters encoded into each candidate solution (i.e., team plan) include 
the number of convolutional layers, filter sizes, number of filters, learning rate, batch size, and dropout rates. Each team 
plan in MLOA represents a unique configuration of these hyperparameters. The optimization process uses classification 
accuracy on the validation set as the primary fitness criterion. During each iteration, MLOA explores diverse combinations 
of these hyperparameters through its leadership-driven refinement strategy. This allows the search to be both guided 
(exploitation) and diverse (exploration) compared to traditional metaheuristics.
Unlike grid search, which exhaustively tests parameter combinations and is computationally expensive, or Bayesian 
optimization, which assumes a probabilistic model of the objective function, MLOA does not rely on prior assump-
tions. Its team-based evolutionary mechanism allows it to explore a larger solution space efficiently. Although other 
metaheuristics (e.g., GA, PSO) have been explored in literature for similar tasks, MLOA was chosen due to its adaptive 
and leadership-inspired design, which reduces the risk of premature convergence and promotes a structured, iterative 
refinement of hyperparameter combinations. Future work will consider a comparative study with other tuning methods 
such as Bayesian optimization or reinforcement learning-based strategies to further validate the choice of MLOA.

5.2  Experimental setup and dataset
The workstation used for this experiment is configured with an Intel i7 CPU, which operates at a base clock speed of 
3.80 GHz and a boost clock speed of 4.12 GHz. This CPU is an 8-core processor that supports 16 threads, providing 
substantial processing power. We incorporated 16 GB of high-speed DDR4 RAM running at 3200 MHz to meet the 
demands of memory-intensive image processing tasks, enabling efficient data handling and processing for large 
datasets. For deep learning endeavors, we harnessed the capabilities of an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2080 GPU equipped 
with 8 GB of GDDR6 VRAM and 2944 CUDA cores. This GPU significantly accelerated neural network training and 
inference, benefiting from a memory bus width of 256 bits. Our GPU-based computations were executed using the 
CUDA Toolkit version 11.1. The research platform was run on the Windows 11 operating system, and we implemented 
and assessed our proposed approach using Python 3.7.10.
The collective utilization of python libraries and the specific hardware configuration allowed us to execute our 
melanoma classification study effectively and efficiently. The computational resources and software tools provided a 
solid foundation for implementing complex algorithms, optimizing hyperparameters, and training CNNs for accurate 
and reliable melanoma identification. By leveraging these resources, we ensured the study’s success and potential 
implications for real-world applications.
5.3  Dataset
For the evaluation of the experiment, two datasets, ­PH2 [33] and the ISIC2020 dataset [34], were used. The use of the 
­PH2 dataset ensures that the dataset for this research should include clinical samples. The ISIC2020 dataset ensures 
that the model can handle a vast volume of data, as ISIC2020 contains 33,126 images. The details of the above-
discussed dataset are given below.
5.3.1  PH2 dataset
The ­PH2 dataset serves the purpose of facilitating research and comparisons in the realm of dermoscopic image 
analysis, catering to both segmentation and classification algorithm evaluations. Originating from the Dermatol-
ogy Service of Hospital Pedro Hispano in Matosinhos, Portugal, this dermoscopic image database was specifically 
acquired using the Tuebinger Mole Analyzer system, maintaining consistent conditions, and utilizing a magnification 
of 20x. The images are 8-bit RGB color representations with a resolution of 768 × 560 pixels. Sample images from the 
­PH2 dataset are provided in Fig. 1.
A total of 200 dermoscopic images were obtained for melanocytic lesions; the ­PH2 database included 80 common 
nevi, 80 atypical nevi, and 40 melanomas. The content of this dataset extends beyond mere images, as it integrates 
comprehensive medical annotations for each entry. These annotations encompass medical segmentation of the 
lesion, clinical and histological diagnoses, and evaluations based on various dermoscopic criteria, including colours, 
pigment network, dots/globules, streaks, regression areas, and the presence of a blue-whitish veil. The meticulous 
inclusion of these annotations enhances the utility of the dataset for in-depth studies and assessments in the field 
of dermatology and dermoscopic image analysis.
5.3.2  ISIC2020 dataset
The dataset for the 2020 SIIM-ISIC Melanoma Classification challenge was meticulously curated to bridge the gap 
between prior challenges and real-world clinical scenarios. Each image in the dataset was uniquely identified, ena-
bling the correlation of lesions from the same patient. This patient-level contextual information holds significant 
clinical value and is commonly employed by clinicians for melanoma diagnosis. This approach proves to be especially 
beneficial for excluding false positives among patients with numerous atypical nevi. The dataset encompasses data 
from 2,056 patients across three continents, with 20.8% having at least one melanoma and 79.2% showing no mela-
nomas. On average, there were 16 lesions per patient, comprising a total of 33,126 dermoscopic images. Notably,

To ensure the generalizability and robustness of the proposed MLOA-optimized CNN model, we implemented a rigorous

ing results across all five folds. For the ISIC2020 dataset, which contains over 33,000 images, we used a stratified split of 
70% training, 15% validation, and 15% testing. Stratification ensured that the class distribution was preserved across 
all subsets.

6.5  Limitation of the proposed approach
While the proposed MLOA shows promising results in optimizing hyperparameters and enhancing CNN models for 
melanoma classification, several limitations should be considered. Firstly, the study primarily focuses on optimizing 
hyperparameters within a controlled experimental setup using benchmark datasets PH2 and ISIC2020. The generaliz-
ability of MLOA to other medical imaging tasks or real-world clinical settings with diverse datasets and varying conditions 
remains to be fully explored. Secondly, while MLOA demonstrates superior performance compared to randomly tuned 
hyperparameters, further comparative studies against state-of-the-art optimization techniques or ensemble methods 
would provide deeper insights into its competitive advantages.
Additionally, the computational resources required for running MLOA may be significant, especially when scaling to 
larger datasets or complex CNN architectures. Future research could explore optimizations to enhance the algorithm’s 
efficiency and scalability. Lastly, the study’s evaluation metrics primarily focus on accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score, 
which are essential but may not capture all aspects of algorithm performance in real-world clinical applications, such 
as interpretability or robustness to noisy data. Addressing these limitations would strengthen the applicability and reli-
ability of MLOA in medical diagnostics and other AI-driven healthcare domains.

7  Conclusion
The MLOA was introduced in this context, drawing inspiration from multiplier leadership principles to optimize complex 
problems. The MLOA has been applied successfully to melanoma classification tasks, significantly enhancing the perfor-
mance of various methods. The algorithm’s transformative process involves posing challenges, fostering collaborative 
discussions, refining ideas, invoking analytical and creative thinking, promoting collaborative decision-making, evaluating 
solutions, and ensuring accountability. MLOA leverages team intelligence and offers a dynamic framework for superior 
problem-solving. The MLOA has also been evaluated for optimizing hyperparameters in CNNs, recognizing the intricate 
relationships within this high-dimensional search space. Hyperparameter configurations are treated like a team’s baseline 
abilities, and the algorithm iteratively explores new configurations while leveraging the concept of team leaders and 
member interactions. The performances of the CNN models trained with the MLOA-optimized hyperparameters out-
perform those trained with the randomly tuned hyperparameters. MLOA achieved remarkable accuracy for melanoma 
classification, with 98.97% using the ­PH2 dataset and 99.47% using the ISIC2020 dataset. Comparisons with existing 
classifiers revealed the superior performance of the MLOA, as demonstrated by accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score 
metrics. Accuracy measures overall correctness, precision signifies accurate identifications, recall indicates the ability to 
identify all relevant instances, and the F1 score balances precision and recall. The effectiveness of the MLOA in optimiz-
ing hyperparameters and CNN models for melanoma classification underscores its potential in various applications.
While the proposed MLOA demonstrates superior performance on benchmark functions and achieves high accuracy 
on melanoma classification, several limitations must be acknowledged. First, the computational cost of MLOA may 
become significant for very high-dimensional optimization problems or large-scale datasets, given its iterative, team-
based design. Second, although the model generalizes well on the PH2 and ISIC2020 datasets, its performance on other 
clinical datasets, especially from different imaging modalities or ethnic groups, remains untested. Third, the real-world 
implementation of the proposed CNN architecture in clinical settings requires integration with hospital IT systems, vali-
dation through clinical trials, and compliance with medical data standards. Addressing these challenges in future work 
will enhance the robustness, scalability, and practical deployment of the proposed approach.

Abstract: This paper proposes the multiplier leadership optimization algorithm, which draws inspiration from multiplier leadership principles to search for and optimize solutions to complex problems effectively. Multiplier leaders possess the unique ability to amplify their teams’ collective intelligence and capabilities. They cultivate an environment of open discussion, creative thinking, accountability, and motivating team members to excel. The proposed algorithm is implemented in MAT- LAB, and its performance is evaluated on the IEEE Congress on Evolutionary Computation 2021 test bench suite, which consists of 80 benchmark functions. The performance of the proposed approach is compared with those of the other 9 other state-of-the-art optimization algorithms. The proposed algorithm successfully solved 47 out of 80 benchmark functions, demonstrating its superior performance. The computational complexity of proposed algorithm is O(M ∗N2) , making it efficient for large-scale problems. Furthermore, this paper proposes an MLOA-based approach to evolve the near-optimal architecture of convolution neural networks for Melanoma classification. The proposed approach is imple- mented in Python and tested on the PH2 and ISIC2020 datasets. The PH2 dataset consists of 200 dermoscopic images, while the ISIC2020 dataset comprises 33,126 images. The proposed approach is compared with 12 other state-of-the-art methods and achieves high classification accuracies of 98.97% on the PH2 dataset and 99.47% on the ISIC2020 dataset. Additional performance metrics include precision of 98.72%, recall of 98.85%, and F1-score of 98.78% on the PH2 data- set, while on the ISIC2020 dataset, it achieves precision of 99.32%, recall of 99.51%, and F1-score of 99.41%. The results indicate that MLOA-based CNN architecture outperforms all existing approaches for Melanoma classification, offering a promising solution for medical image analysis. Article Highlights • Introduces MLOA, a novel optimization method inspired by multiplier leadership principles. • MLOA outperforms 9 existing algorithms across benchmark functions. • Achieves superior Melanoma classification accuracies up to 99.47% on diverse datasets.
